title: Infection Prevention and Control
summary: Learn to prevent infections in care settings: the chain of infection, standard precautions and hand hygiene, PPE and transmission-based precautions, cleaning and disinfection, waste and sharps safety, and surveillance.
audience: Nurses, clinic staff, cleaners, care workers, health students and community health workers

lessons.title: How infections spread in care settings

body.p: Infection prevention and control (IPC) protects patients, health workers and visitors from infections acquired during care. Health-care-associated infections, such as surgical-site infections, catheter-related urinary infections and pneumonia, prolong illness, increase costs and cause deaths, and many are preventable.

list: Infectious agent: bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites.
Reservoir: where it lives, such as people, water, equipment or surfaces.
Portal of exit: how it leaves, such as coughing, blood or faeces.
Mode of transmission: contact (hands, equipment), droplets, airborne particles, or blood and body fluids.
Portal of entry: broken skin, mouth, airway, catheters.
Susceptible host: especially newborns, older people and people with weakened immunity or invasive devices.

body.p: Every IPC practice breaks one or more links. Hand hygiene interrupts contact transmission; vaccination of health workers reduces susceptible hosts; cleaning removes reservoirs.

body.tip: For any procedure, ask: which link of the chain am I breaking with each step?

body.p: Standard precautions apply to every patient, every time, because infection status is often unknown. They include hand hygiene, appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), respiratory hygiene, safe injection practices, safe handling of sharps, environmental cleaning, and safe handling of linen and waste.

body.h: WHO's five moments for hand hygiene

steps: Before a clean or aseptic procedure.

list: Alcohol-based hand rub takes about 20 to 30 seconds and is preferred when hands are not visibly dirty.
Soap and water takes about 40 to 60 seconds and is needed when hands are visibly soiled, and after caring for patients with some infections such as C. difficile diarrhoea.
Keep nails short, remove rings and watches, and cover cuts.

body.p: Observers record opportunities and actions. If staff performed hand hygiene at 85 of 120 observed opportunities, compliance is 85 / 120, about 70.8%, showing room to improve.

body.tip: Place hand rub at the point of care, within arm's reach of every bed; convenience strongly increases compliance.

body.p: PPE protects health workers and patients when used correctly. Choose it according to the risk of exposure: gloves for contact with blood, body fluids or broken skin; aprons or gowns to protect clothing; masks and eye protection for splashes or respiratory infections; respirators (such as N95 or FFP2) for airborne infections.

list: A common order for putting on: hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves.
A common order for removal: gloves, hand hygiene, eye protection, gown, mask or respirator, then hand hygiene again; follow your facility's procedure.
Removal is when contamination most often happens: touch only the clean parts, slowly.
Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, and the same gloves must not be used for different patients.
Contact precautions (for example for multidrug-resistant organisms): gloves and gown, dedicated equipment.
Droplet precautions (for example influenza): mask within close range, spacing patients.
Airborne precautions (for example tuberculosis, measles): respirators, well-ventilated or negative-pressure rooms, and keeping doors closed.

body.tip: Practise putting on and removing PPE with a colleague watching; small mistakes are easy to miss on your own.

body.p: Items and surfaces need different levels of processing, according to the infection risk of how they are used (often called the Spaulding classification).

list: Critical items entering sterile tissue or blood (surgical instruments) must be sterilised, for example by steam autoclave.
Semi-critical items touching mucous membranes (some endoscopes) need high-level disinfection at least.
Non-critical items touching intact skin (blood-pressure cuffs, bed rails) need cleaning and low-level disinfection.
Cleaning to remove visible dirt always comes first; disinfectants do not work well through dirt.

body.p: Chlorine (bleach) solutions are widely used. To dilute a 5% stock solution to 0.5% (for blood spills and some surfaces), mix 1 part bleach with 9 parts water (5 / 10 = 0.5%). For 0.1% (general surfaces), mix 1 part with 49 parts water (5 / 50 = 0.1%). For example, 100 mL of 5% bleach made up to 1 litre (adding 900 mL of water) gives 0.5%. Make fresh solutions daily, label them and wear gloves; follow your facility's protocol and product label.

body.tip: Clean from cleaner areas to dirtier areas, and from high surfaces to low, so you do not spread contamination.

body.p: Most health-care waste is general waste, but a share is hazardous: infectious waste, sharps, pathological waste, chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Poor handling exposes staff, waste handlers and communities to infection and injury.

list: Use colour-coded bins according to national guidelines, for example separate containers for general, infectious and sharps waste.
Place sharps immediately into puncture-resistant sharps containers; never recap needles by hand.
Close sharps containers when about three-quarters full.
Store waste securely and treat it by approved methods (autoclaving, incineration) before disposal.

body.p: Wash the area immediately with soap and water (or flush eyes and mucous membranes with water), report at once, and get assessed for post-exposure prophylaxis, which for HIV should start as soon as possible, ideally within hours. Health workers should be vaccinated against hepatitis B.

body.tip: Most sharps injuries happen after use and during disposal; dispose of the sharp yourself, immediately, at the point of use.

body.p: IPC programmes need leadership, trained staff, guidelines, supplies, monitoring and feedback. WHO's core components include an IPC programme and team, guidelines, education, surveillance of infections, multimodal improvement strategies, monitoring and feedback, adequate staffing and bed occupancy, and a safe built environment with water, sanitation and supplies.

list: Cumulative incidence: 12 surgical-site infections among 800 operations is 12 / 800 = 1.5%.
Incidence density: 12 infections over 4000 patient-days is 12 / 4000 x 1000 = 3 per 1000 patient-days, useful for device-related infections.
Audits of practices such as hand hygiene, catheter care and cleaning.
Feedback of results to teams, which drives improvement.

body.p: Antimicrobial stewardship programmes work alongside IPC: preventing infections reduces antibiotic use, and careful antibiotic use reduces resistant organisms that are hard to control.

body.tip: Share infection and audit data with ward teams regularly; people improve what they can see.

quiz.q: Which is a link in the chain of infection?

options: Only patients known to be infected

quiz.q: Which is one of WHO's five moments for hand hygiene?
options: Before a clean or aseptic procedure

quiz.q: An alcohol hand rub should take about:
Hand hygiene at 85 of 120 opportunities is compliance of about:
Surgical instruments entering sterile tissue must be:
To make 0.5% chlorine from 5% bleach, mix 1 part bleach with:
What must happen before disinfecting a surface?

options: Placed immediately in a sharps container without recapping

quiz.q: After a needlestick injury you should first:
options: Apply a bandage and keep working without reporting
Wait to see if symptoms appear
Wash with soap and water and report immediately
